title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards

paper.title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards
paper.abstract: Abstract Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose Lean4AgenticRL , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. Lean4AgenticRL first builds a problem-specific workflow system that balances the agent’s own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using Lean4AgenticRL , we train LAR-9B/27B , a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of the similar size. LAR-27B achieves 77.3% on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by 9.89% and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by 5.07% . These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform long-running agentic tasks has been regarded as a key capability by the computer science community ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . This capability is typically evaluated by solving complex software engineering (SWE) ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) and terminal-usage ( Team, 2025c ) tasks within advanced harness frameworks ( Anthropic, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2025 ; Merrill & Shaw, 2025 ) . Given the significant practical value ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , training advanced agentic LLMs has become an important research direction. Agentic capability in LLMs refers to the model’s ability to actively interact with an environment to explore, understand, and resolve tasks. Previous works have developed multiple approaches to strengthen this ability, including simple prompting ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ) and building supervised fine-tuning datasets ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Badertdinov et al., 2026 ) . Building on the success of scaling Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) and multi-turn agentic RL methods ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ) , the community has driven significant progress in long-horizon agent tasks such as SWE and terminal-usage. Figure 1: Overview of Lean4AgenticRL framework: The Lean4AgenticRL framework contains three major steps: (a) Problem-specific workflow agent system : A plan-then-execute process that first explores and produces the problem-specific workflow (PSWF). Then execute the PSWF to solve the task. (b) Workflow Formalization and Multi-level Reward Annotation : An annotation process that formalizes the PSWF into our generalized Lean4Agent framework. Then segment the agent trajectory into workflow stages, and assign mid-level workflow-stage rewards and low-level toolcall rewards. (c) Lean4AgenticRL training : We apply the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithms to train the LLM agent with multi-level rewards. Despite significant progress in large-scale agentic RL, reliably assigning process rewards in long agent traces remains an open problem. In particular, current agentic RL methods ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026 ) primarily rely on high-level outcome rewards, building on their success in single-turn RLVR. However, these signals do not directly distinguish useful intermediate actions from incorrect or redundant steps within successful trajectories, limiting the effectiveness of training ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . This has motivated the use of process rewards to supervise the agent’s intermediate steps ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Xi et al., 2026 ) . However, existing approaches often focus on low-level toolcall results, which may overlook broader workflow progress and degrade performance when a single toolcall cannot directly connect to the task objectives ( Modecrua et al., 2026 ) . Overall, these limitations highlight the need to unify the high-level outcome rewards, mid-level workflow-stage rewards, and low-level toolcall rewards in a verifiable way to enable more effective agentic RL. To address the above limitations, we propose Lean4AgenticRL , a unified framework for deriving multi-level rewards within a uniform, Lean4Agent verifiable, open-ended agentic RL setting. The overview of Lean4AgenticRL is presented in Figure 1 . In Lean4AgenticRL , we first use problem-specific workflow (PSWF) agent system that balances the agent’s inherent capabilities with execution controls through a plan-then-execute paradigm. It further provides the basis for verifying agent behaviors. Subsequently, we extend the Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) verification framework from fixed workflows to general harnesses. Then, we formalize the PSWF and segment the agent trajectories into formal workflow stages and annotate the trajectories with high-level outcome rewards ( α \alpha ), mid-level workflow-stage rewards ( β \beta ), and low-level toolcall rewards ( γ \gamma ). These reward signals synergistically support learning from both final outcomes and intermediate behaviors through our workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm, enabling more effective agentic RL. We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We propose Lean4AgenticRL , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards within Lean, a uniform dependent-type verifiable language, for agentic RL in open-ended domains that enables more effective agentic RL. (2) We develop problem-specific workflow and generalize the current agent verification framework from fixed workflow to general harness systems. They greatly enlarge the applicability of the current uniform formal agent verification system. (3) We train LAR-9B/27B through Lean4AgenticRL . Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of comparable size on SWE and general terminal-usage tasks. LAR-27B achieves 77.3% on TerminalBench-2.1 ( Team, 2025c ) and, across the three benchmarks we evaluated, our model outperforms their base model by 9.89% and the second-best models of comparable size by 5.07% on average. The performance highlights the effectiveness and generality of Lean4AgenticRL . Furthermore, Lean4AgenticRL offers a new view of agentic RL methods grounded in formal verification and provides a unified framework for future studies to explore applications of formal methods within the modern RL paradigm. To facilitate the advancement of the fields, our code and model have been open-sourced in https://github.com/RickySkywalker/Lean4AgenticRL

sections.heading: 2 Methodology
sections.text: We detail the formulation of the Lean4AgenticRL framework in this section. The goal of Lean4AgenticRL is to derive multi-level rewards in a uniform Lean schema to achieve more effective agentic RL in open-ended domains. Section 2.1 introduces the key preliminaries, Section 2.2 details the formulation of Problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system, Section 2.3 introduces the workflow formalization and reward annotation method, and Section 2.4 shows how we train the model using the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO method.

sections.heading: 2.1 Preliminaries
sections.text: In this section, we introduce the central preliminary concept for Lean4AgenticRL . Additionally, we present the definitions of the terms we used in the paper in Appendix B . LLM Agent Following ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , we define an LLM agent as an LLM-based system that cycles between reasoning with tool-based actions. The reasoning enables the agent to formulate, track, and revise its plan, while actions allow it to interact with environments to execute external tools or read information sources. In our paper, we use Claude-code ( Anthropic, 2026a ) or Terminus-2 ( Merrill & Shaw, 2025 ) as our agent harness. Lean4Agent Verification System Following Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , we present the workflow for the LLM agent as a heterogeneous directed graph 𝒢 = ⟨ V , E ⟩ \mathcal{G}=\langle V,E\rangle , where V := { v i } i = 1 m V:=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} contains the workflow stages and E ⊆ V × V E\subseteq V\times V specifies the allowed transitions between stages. The Lean4Agent system implements a set of pre-conditions ρ i ( p ​ r ​ e ) \rho_{i}^{(pre)} and post-conditions ρ i ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho_{i}^{(post)} with the predicates , which describe atomic properties of the agent behaviors. When executing the workflow, we obtain trajectory 𝝉 \bm{\tau} , and each stage i ∈ [ 1 , m ] i\in[1,m] has its trajectory 𝝉 i = { τ i , j } \bm{\tau}_{i}=\{\tau_{i,j}\} . The trajectory-level verification evaluates whether its entry and exit states satisfy ρ i ( p ​ r ​ e ) \rho_{i}^{(pre)} and ρ i ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho_{i}^{(post)} , respectively. These predicate-based specifications, combined with a dependent-type formal foundation, provide the verification of workflow-level coherence and assess completion of the specified stages’ goals. Following Lean4Agent, in this work, we define a stage as verified when its Lean4Agent workflow specification’s post-condition holds over after the stage’s execution.

sections.heading: 2.2 Problem-specific Workflow Agent System
sections.text: This section introduces the problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system. It aims to balance the controllability of fixed-workflow execution against the flexibility of free-form, ReAct-style execution. It also lays the foundation for our further verification process. In particular, we achieve this by a plan-then-execute paradigm.

sections.heading: 2.2.1 Planning Phase
sections.text: In this phase, we apply the LLM as the planning agent within the agent harness to explore the task environment and formulate a PSWF. Formally, given the problem statement 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , its environment ℰ \mathcal{E} (commonly a container), and a general workflow 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , we obtain the PSWF 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{S}} as follows: 𝒲 𝒮 , 𝝉 ( p ) = H ​ ( L ​ L ​ M ​ ( ℰ , 𝒮 , 𝒲 ) ) \mathcal{W_{S}},\bm{\tau}^{(p)}=\text{H}(LLM(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W})) where H ( ⋅ ) (\cdot) denotes the agent harness and 𝝉 ( p ) \bm{\tau}^{(p)} denotes the trajectory for planning phase. The 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W_{S}} is a natural-language plan that specializes in stage-wise guidance in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} based on the findings from its exploration. For example, in SWE tasks, it contains detailed information such as relevant source files, suspected causes of the issue, and proposed repair and verification steps, providing concrete instructions for subsequent execution. The PSWF aims to control the agent behavior without limiting its flexibility.

sections.heading: 2.2.2 Execution Phase
sections.text: In this phase, we execute the PSWF 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{S}} in its task environment ℰ \mathcal{E} by instructing the LLM agent. To avoid repeated exploration, we also include the planning-phase trajectory 𝝉 ( p ) \bm{\tau}^{(p)} in the context. Formally, we have: ℰ ′ , 𝝉 ( e ) = H ​ ( L ​ L ​ M ​ ( ℰ , 𝒲 𝒮 , 𝝉 ( p ) ) ) \mathcal{E}^{\prime},\bm{\tau}^{(e)}=\text{H}(LLM(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{W_{S}},\bm{\tau}^{(p)})) where ℰ ′ \mathcal{E}^{\prime} is the updated environment to resolve the problem and 𝝉 ( e ) = { τ i } i = 1 n \bm{\tau}^{(e)}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} records the execution steps. Alongside the planning phase, we complete the rollout of our agentic RL and lay the foundation for subsequent multi-reward assignment based on the agent verification system.

sections.heading: 2.3 Workflow Formalization and Multi-level Reward Annotation
sections.text: In this section, we introduce methods for adapting a formal verification system beyond a fixed workflow schema via the PSWF formalization, and detail methods for annotating multi-level rewards based on the formalized workflow and execution trajectory.

sections.heading: 2.3.1 Generalizing Agent Verification System with PSWF
sections.text: The current agent verification framework that can uniformly process both workflow and trajectory levels, such as Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , is designed for predefined, fixed workflows. However, most modern agent harnesses are open-ended without such fixed workflows. Thus, to make Lean4AgenticRL applicable to a broader domain, we propose methods to generalize the verification framework with PSWF. Although 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{S}} provides stage-wise guidance for 𝝉 ( e ) \bm{\tau}^{(e)} , the correspondence between agent steps and workflow stages must be determined from annotation. Each stage is also aligned with the general workflow 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , ensuring the stages remain comparable across rollouts. Here, each agent step either remains in the current stage or transitions to one of the connected stages. Since every decision depends only on the local window, not the full rollout, the segmentation scales to ultra-long trajectories. For loops and branches, each revisit of a stage is treated as a separate instance with its own index. Consequently, each stage i i obtains its step set { τ i , j } j = 1 n i ⊆ 𝝉 ( e ) \{\tau_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}\subseteq\bm{\tau}^{(e)} , where n i n_{i} denotes the number of steps assigned to it. Together, the formalized workflow and step-to-stage alignment allow the formal agent verification to move beyond fixed workflow to general agent harnesses.

sections.heading: 2.3.2 Workflow-Stage Mid-level Reward Annotation
sections.text: After the execution trajectory is segmented into workflow stages. Following Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , we annotate the workflow-stage mid-level reward β \beta by verifying that each stage accomplishes its specified goals, represented as functions of predicates. This reward serves as the middle ground between the low-level toolcall rewards and high-level outcome rewards. The former is prone to overlooking broader workflow progress, and the latter cannot verify the correctness of intermediate actions. Specifically, for each stage i i , we examine whether the steps { τ i , j } j = 1 n i \{\tau_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}} entered the specified pre-condition ρ i ( p ​ r ​ e ) \rho^{(pre)}_{i} and established the desired post-condition ρ i ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho^{(post)}_{i} . Directly decidable predicates are verified through Lean or Python code, while those requiring semantic interpretation are assessed by an LLM judge. The boundary for the formal components in our system is discussed in Appendix F . Formally, the workflow β \beta reward can be defined as: If ρ ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho^{(post)} ’s additional predicate requirements are satisfied upon the exit of stage i i , then β = 1 \beta=1 , otherwise, β = − 1 \beta=-1 . The detailed reward annotation schema is provided in Appendix I.1 .

sections.heading: 2.3.3 Toolcall Low-level Reward Annotation
sections.text: Since part of the predicate judgment in β \beta rewards relies on LLM-as-judge verification, the policy may learn to hack the reward through ritualistic behaviors rather than resolving the task. For example, to satisfy the predicate that requires repeated fix-and-retry attempts, the agent can simply rerun the same testing bash command several times and thereby mislead the judge. To address this issue, we further extend the formal predicate system from the workflow level to a finer-grained toolcall level. Specifically, we implement a set of symbolic predicates, including consecutive_repetition , noop_commands , const_shell , ⋯ \cdots , and evaluate them using Lean and Python checkers to target these common reward-hacking patterns. The full list of penalized behaviors is presented in Appendix I.2 . With this annotation, each step τ i \tau_{i} receives a low-level toolcall reward γ i ∈ { − 1 , 0 } \gamma_{i}\in\{-1,0\} . Here, we deliberately set γ \gamma to a penalty-only reward that punishes violations of the step without granting any positive reward, so the policy cannot exploit γ \gamma itself to overwhelm other positive rewards. Consequently, we obtain a symbolic guard that largely prevents most commonly observed reward-hacking strategies against β \beta .

sections.heading: 2.4 Lean4AgenticRL Training
sections.text: With the multi-level rewards in place, we unify the β \beta and γ \gamma rewards with the verifier-based outcome reward α \alpha with the enhanced Lean4Agent formal framework that jointly manages all the rewards in a single reward server for scalable agentic RL. We apply this reward to optimize the policy with our variant of GRPO ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , namely workflow-stage-normalized GRPO . Those are the groups that receive less stable gradients from outcome rewards, whereas our method can provide richer process rewards. sections.heading: 2.5 Summary
sections.text: To provide a clear overview of the Lean4AgenticRL training framework, we present the complete framework as pseudocode in Appendix C . We apply the Lean4AgenticRL training to train a family model named LAR-9B/27B ( Agentic RL Model with Process Reward with Lean 4 ) on the software-engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage tasks.

sections.heading: 3 Experiment
sections.text: We validate the effectiveness of Lean4AgenticRL and the performance of LAR-9B/27B model based on SWE-Bench-Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 ( Team, 2025c ) . Specifically, we present the main results in Section 3.3 and compare the training dynamics with outcome-reward GRPO in Section 3.4 . Subsequently, we conduct ablation studies in Section 3.5 and case study in Section 3.6 . We also perform additional experiments in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Task and Benchmark
sections.text: We assess the LAR models in two advanced agentic tasks, namely, software engineering (SWE) and general terminal usage. They are measured by SWE-Bench-Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) and TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 ( Team, 2025c ) , both of which are widely adopted in evaluating frontier LLMs ( Qwen Team, 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026c ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026 ) . We evaluate on SWE-Bench-Verified under mean@3, and on TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 under mean@5, using randomized seeds. Further details on the benchmarks and tasks are presented in Appendix G .

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Baselines
sections.text: To evaluate the effectiveness of the Lean4AgenticRL and the LAR-9B/27B models, we compare them with the latest open-weight models of similar size. Following previous works ( Ivison et al., 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ) , for the 9B model, we mainly compared with OpenThinker-Agent-V1 ( Team, 2025a ) , Qwen-3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , TMax-9B ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) , and Gemma-4-12B ( Farabet & Lacombe, 2026 ) . The 27B-level model is compared with Qwen-3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) , TMax-27B ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) , Qwen-3-Coder-30B ( Team, 2025b ) Gemma-4-31B ( Farabet & Lacombe, 2026 ) , and Qwen-3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026c ) . All the baselines run with the highest reasoning effort and the longest supported context length to elicit their best performance. For the agent harness, we report the results on Terminus-2 ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) for TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 and Claude-code ( Anthropic, 2026a ) for SWE-Bench-Verified.

sections.heading: 3.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: We train the LAR-9B/27B based on Qwen-3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) and Qwen-3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026c ) using a mixture of TMax-15k ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) and SWE-ReBench ( Badertdinov et al., 2026 ) dataset. Training is performed with asynchronous RL built on SLIME ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) and OpenClaw-RL ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . The 9B model is trained for 160 steps, and the 27B model for 120 steps. Both with a batch size of 32 and group size of 32 ( 32 × 32 ) (32\times 32) following GLM-5 ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Follwoing the clip-higher strategy ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , we set ε u = 0.28 \varepsilon_{u}=0.28 and ε l = 0.2 \varepsilon_{l}=0.2 and we use a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} for both models. The maximum context length is set to 128K tokens with each response capped at 8K tokens. The training is conducted on a 64-H200 GPU cluster and takes 160 and 240 hours for the 9B and 27B models, respectively. Following Lean4Agent, we apply v4.20.0 for Lean and Mathlib. sections.heading: 3.3 Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 presents the results of LAR-9B/27B compared against open-weights models of similar size. At 9B scale, LAR-9B improves on its base model by 20.2% , 13.5% , and 13.4% on SWE-Bench-Verified, TerminalBench-2.0 and 2.1 with paired-p-value of average improvement < 10 − 10 <10^{-10} . It also surpasses the second-best model of comparable size by 10.7% , 5.6% , and 1.9% on those benchmarks with p = 3.5 × 10 − 3 p=3.5\times 10^{-3} . Notably, LAR-9B even exceeds the much larger Gemma-4-31B on SWE-Bench-Verified and performs on par with it on TerminalBench-2.0. At 27B scale, LAR-27B further raises the baseline’s performance by 1.2% , 3.5% , and 7.7% on the three benchmarks respectively with p = 0.044 p=0.044 , reaching 84.2% on SWE-Bench-Verified and 77.3% on TerminalBench-2.1 1 1 1 At 27B scale, SWE-Bench-Verified is approaching saturation and TerminalBench-2.0 consists tasks whose external dependencies are inaccessible ( The Terminal-Bench Team, 2026 ) , which makes TB-2.1 offering a more reliable comparison at this scale. . In general, LAR family models achieve the best results at both scales across all three benchmarks, significantly outperforming their base models by 9.89% and the second-best model by 5.07% on average. These gains indicate that Lean4AgenticRL can provide more effective agentic RL that continuously optimizes models that have already undergone extensive post-training. We attribute this to the multi-level reward design, which obtains training signals from groups that originally produce less desirable gradients, thereby yielding more informative training signals.

sections.heading: 3.4 Compared with Direct RL Training
sections.text: In this section, we investigate the performance of Lean4AgenticRL compared to normal GRPO-based agentic RL using pure outcome rewards under the OpenClaw-RL ( Wang et al., 2026c ) framework. In particular, we conducted the training with a 16 × 16 16\times 16 step size using SWE-ReBench ( Badertdinov et al., 2026 ) for 30 steps on the SWE task, or TMax ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) for 80 steps on the terminal-usage task, both based on Qwen-3.5-9B. Throughout the training, we evaluate the intermediate checkpoint on SWE-Bench-Verified with pass@1 and on TerminalBench-2.0 with mean@3. The training dynamics are presented in Figure 2 . The results show that Lean4AgenticRL outperforms the GRPO baseline throughout training on both tasks. On the SWE task, GRPO improves during the first 15 steps but then quickly deteriorates, falling back to roughly its initial level by step 20, while Lean4AgenticRL improves steadily over all 30 steps. We hypothesize that pure outcome rewards may reward some intermediate steps that are not functioning as desired, thereby destabilizing training at a later stage. In the terminal usage task, GRPO fluctuates substantially and improves slowly, with a pronounced mid-task degradation, whereas Lean4AgenticRL maintains a clear upward trend with a consistent margin. Moreover, Lean4AgenticRL is more efficient in terms of training steps; it surpasses the best GRPO checkpoint within 10 steps on SWE and 30 steps on terminal-usage. sections.heading: 3.5.1 Dropping Problem-Specific Workflow
sections.text: We first examine whether the PSWF system itself benefits the agent execution without training. Specifically, we evaluate Qwen-3.5-9B on SWE-Bench-Verified in the Claude-code harness, with or without the PSWF. The results are shown in Table 2 , which shows that removing PSWF reduces the resolution rate from 44.0% to 42.4%. When we take a closer look at the failed trajectories, we observe that without PSWF guidance, the agent often explores the repository insufficiently, fails to locate the relevant files, and misattributes the root cause of the issue. This experiment demonstrates that, rather than limiting the agent’s capabilities, applying the PSWF alone can improve the performance of LLM agents.

sections.heading: 3.5.2 Dropping γ \gamma rewards
sections.text: Table 2: Ablation Studies Result Method SWE-Bench-Verified w/o γ \gamma 49.4% w/ γ \gamma 56.0% w/o PSWF 42.4% w/ PSWF 44.0% This experiment aims to assess the role of γ \gamma by repeating the 30-step SWE training in Section 3.4 with γ \gamma removed from the reward, while keeping all other settings unchanged. As shown in Table 2 , removing γ \gamma reduces the performance of the model by 6.6%. It also increases the number of repeated commands captured by γ \gamma by 66.8% compared to the base model, while the full Lean4AgenticRL training observed almost no such behavior. Removing γ \gamma also increases the total number of tool calls by 18.7% compared to the full Lean4AgenticRL . Without this guard, the policy quickly learns to hack the LLM-as-judge predicates in β \beta through ritualistic actions, such as echo and repeated read-only or placeholder commands. As the training proceeds, these actions fill the context and inflate the response length with little contribution to the solutions. In contrast, with γ \gamma in place, the response length of Lean4AgenticRL grows steadily alongside its performance, and we observed almost no reward hacking activities guarded by γ \gamma . These results confirm the necessity of the low-level toolcall rewards γ \gamma .

sections.heading: 3.6 Case Study
sections.text: This section illustrates the signal that our multi-level rewards provide during training. We evaluate the base model and the step-40, 80, and 120 checkpoints of LAR-27B on TerminalBench-2.1 ( Team, 2025c ) and annotate their trajectories using the training reward pipeline, as if they were rollouts in a group that receives process rewards. In particular, we select the regex-chess results at those checkpoints as the case we demonstrate. The detailed case is demonstrated in Appendix J . As shown in Table 4 , the binary outcome reward α \alpha stays at − 1 -1 for the first three checkpoints and cannot distinguish them. In contrast, the fraction of stages with β = + 1 \beta=+1 rises from 2/8 to 4/7 and 5/6 before the task is solved at step 120 (5/5), while the model also writes fewer stages as training proceeds. When taking a closer look at the trajectories in Figures 6 , 7 , 8 , and 9 , we can see that the workflow-stage reward accurately identifies the intermediate failures and successes. This case illustrates that β \beta can provide a denser signal than α \alpha before a task is solved, and to some extent demonstrates the mechanism of Lean4AgenticRL ’s multi-level reward through detailed cases.

sections.heading: 4.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a scalable approach to enhancing LLM capabilities. It was first scaled by OpenAI-O1 ( OpenAI, 2024 ) and open-sourced by DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and Kimi-K1.5 ( Team et al., 2025 ) . RLVR shows that simple verifier-based outcome rewards can elicit reasoning capabilities without learning reward models. Building on this paradigm, agentic RL extends it to multi-turn agent interactions, typically rewarding the correctness of the final answer or task success ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ) . However, as the agent’s task extends over a longer horizon, sparse outcome rewards that assign identical credit to every step cannot distinguish useful intermediate actions from redundant or erroneous ones. To provide denser training signals, subsequent studies apply process rewards on individual tool calls or infer step-level rewards from LLM judges ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . However, these signals are largely tied to low-level tool calls, which overlook broader progress and may even impair optimization ( Modecrua et al., 2026 ) . Prior work on hierarchical credit assignment ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) relies on highly similar trajectories or tree-search methods, a setting that differs substantially from open-ended tasks such as SWE and general terminal usage. A separate line of work replaces LLM judges with symbolic or algorithmic oracles as verifiable process rewards, but those oracles act as task-specific verifiers in controlled environments ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . In contrast, Lean4AgenticRL derives verifiable rewards across multiple levels under a unified formal language framework for general, open-ended agent executions.

sections.heading: 4.2 Verifiable Agent Systems
sections.text: As agentic systems mature and are increasingly deployed in high-stakes, long-horizon tasks, a growing line of work aims to formally model and verify agent behaviors. Some frameworks provide a type-based linter for the agent workflow that is embedded in agent languages ( Chase, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , while others verify tool calls and their execution results ( Miculicich et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) . More recently, Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) formalizes agent behavior from workflow to execution in Lean, but it relies on predefined, fixed workflow settings. In contrast to theorem proving ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) and code verification ( Li et al., 2026 ) , where formal verifiers routinely supply training signals, these agent verifications serve only as runtime checks or post-hoc audits.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper presents Lean4AgenticRL , to the best of our knowledge, the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards under a unified framework based on Lean4, an expressive dependent-type formal language, for open-ended agentic RL. Its problem-specific workflow agent system balances the agent’s inherent capability with execution controllability. Lean4AgenticRL proposes the workflow formalization methods that extend agent verification beyond fixed workflows to general harnesses. Built on this foundation, Lean4AgenticRL unifies high-level outcome rewards ( α \alpha ), mid-level workflow-stage rewards ( β \beta ), and low-level toolcall rewards ( γ \gamma ). It also proposes the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm, which aims to resolve the grouping problem in agentic RL. We train the LAR-9B/27B models using Lean4AgenticRL . Extensive experiments on SWE-Bench-Verified, TerminalBench-2.0, and 2.1 indicate that they outperform their base models by an average of 9.89% and the second-best model we know on those domains by 5.07% . To the best of our knowledge, LAR-9B/27B achieves the best results among models with comparable size. More broadly, Lean4AgenticRL lays a foundation for integrating verifiable symbolic signals into LLM training and points towards a new paradigm for agentic RL.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: Despite the strong results achieved by Lean4AgenticRL , our framework still has some limitations. Firstly, Lean4AgenticRL ’s verifiability still relies on explicitly bounding agent behavior externally; it does not open the black box of LLM’s internal computation to achieve thorough and transparent verification. Secondly, the scope of this work is limited to designing better rewards for agentic RL, without integrating the verification into the harness system at runtime. Finally, Lean4AgenticRL primarily focuses on traditional agentic tasks, such as SWE or general terminal usage, without incorporating visual signals into the RL process.

sections.heading: Appendix B Term Definitions
sections.text: Since the verifiable agent framework through dependent-type language like Lean is a new domain that may not be widely known by the community, we present the definition of the terms in this section: 1. Lean 4: Lean 4 is a functional programming language and interactive theorem prover based on dependent type theory, whose trusted kernel mechanically checks the correctness of programs and proofs; in Lean4AgenticRL , leveraging the foundation library established in Lean4Agent 2.3.1 , we use it as the shared formal foundation for building formal representations for workflows and unifying the multi-level reward signals. 2. Dependent type language: A dependent type language, such as Lean, allows types to depend on values, so that a single language can express both programs and precise mathematical statements about them, and, under the Curry-Howard correspondence ( Sørensen & Urzyczyn, 2006 ) , verifying a proof reduces to type-checking a term against the type of the statement it proves. 3. Agent workflow: A structured plan for solving a task, represented as a directed graph 𝒢 = ⟨ V , E ⟩ \mathcal{G}=\langle V,E\rangle whose nodes V V are workflow stages and whose edges E ⊆ V × V E\subseteq V\times V specify the allowed transitions between them, including sequential, branching, and loop-back transitions. In Lean4AgenticRL , we also refer to the natural-language PSWF, which carries this structure implicitly, as a workflow. 4. Workflow stage: A node v i ∈ V v_{i}\in V of the workflow graph that represents a sub-goal of the task (e.g., reproducing the issue or verifying the fix) is called a workflow stage. 5. Agent step: A single reasoning-action cycle of the agent, consisting of its reasoning, the toolcalls, and the observation of results, which serves as the atomic unit of a trajectory and the granularity at which the γ \gamma rewards are assigned. Typically, a workflow stage consists of a sequence of agent steps. 6. Semantic predicates for agent: Following Lean4Agent Wang et al. (2026b) , it is atomic decidable typed functions on the agent’s execution state and trajectory evidence that describe atomic properties of agent behavior. The property can be verified by Lean or Python code when it is directly decidable, and by an evidence-grounded LLM judge when semantic interpretation is required. 7. Pre-/post-conditions: Functions of predicates attached to each workflow stage v i v_{i} , where the pre-condition ρ i ( pre ) \rho_{i}^{(\mathrm{pre})} specifies what must hold when the agent enters the stage and the post-condition ρ i ( post ) \rho_{i}^{(\mathrm{post})} specifies what the stage must establish upon exit, analogous to a Hoare triple { ρ i ( pre ) } ​ v i ​ { ρ i ( post ) } \{\rho_{i}^{(\mathrm{pre})}\}\ v_{i}\ \{\rho_{i}^{(\mathrm{post})}\} .

sections.heading: D.1 Applying Lean4AgenticRL training to additional models
sections.text: To demonstrate the effectiveness of Lean4AgenticRL , besides Qwen-3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) and Qwen-3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026c ) , we also apply the training method to Qwen-3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) for 80 steps and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-304B ( Xu et al., 2026 ) for 40 steps using TMax ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) dataset following the exact same training recipes. For Qwen-3.6-27B base model, we evaluate the results using SWE-Bench-Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) and TerminalBench-2.0 ( Team, 2025c ) . The base model’s performance is 70.0% and 45.6%, respectively, while the trained model yields 74.0% and 53.6% on the results. This indicates an improvement of 4.0% on the SWE task and 8.0% on the terminal-usage task. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-304B, the base model achieves 67.3% on TerminalBench-2.1, while our trained model achieves 72.9%, representing a 5.6% improvement. These results indicate that the effectiveness of the Lean4AgenticRL training methods is consistent across model size, model family, and post-training variants. It further demonstrates the potential of further scaling the Lean4AgenticRL process reward to frontier models in significantly larger sizes.

sections.heading: D.2 Faithfulness of Workflow Annotation
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate the faithfulness of our LLM-based annotations during Lean4AgenticRL . In particular, we have the following three main parts of LLM-as-judge annotation in our framework: • Predicate annotation faithfulness: In this type of faithfulness, we evaluate whether the generated workflow in our problem-specific workflow (PSWF) stage has the correct workflow annotation. In particular, we evaluate whether it annotates correct pre- and post-conditions using the correct predicate. The annotation fails in this step if it misses some important predicates. For example, if the acceptance_criteria predicate required by the PSWF is missing from the postcondition of the corresponding workflow stage, the annotation is counted as a failure. • Workflow segmentation faithfulness: This type of faithfulness mainly verifies whether our segmentation process faithfully segmented the execution tool calls into the corresponding general workflow steps. The annotation fails at this step if the segmentation of tool calls spans significantly different workflow steps. For example, if one tool call in SWE agents is writing patches to fix the program, but it is classified as the write_test workflow stage, then it is a failure. • Trajectory verification faithfulness: It mainly covers the faithfulness of the process for our actual annotation of β \beta rewards with the trajectory. One annotation is counted as a failure if this workflow stage is judged a failure by a human/external LLM judge, but it provides β \beta rewards during training and vice versa. For example, if the implement_fix workflow step fails to generate a correct fix for the SWE workflow, but in the training Lean4AgenticRL reward judgments provide β \beta reward to that step, then it is counted as a failure. Table 3: LLM-based evaluation of workflow annotation faithfulness Faithfulness Type Failure Rate Predicate annotation 8.03% Workflow segmentation 6.21% Trajectory verification 4.84% In particular, the author team first manually evaluated a sample of 10 workflows to develop the judgment criteria for the three levels of faithfulness, and then applied Claude-code with Fable-5.1 ( Anthropic, 2026b ) to annotate 1,200 trajectories from our training set. In total, for predicate annotation faithfulness , we evaluated 32,295 predicate annotations, and for workflow segmentation faithfulness , we evaluated 20,235 steps that segmented into 5,912 workflow stages, and for trajectory verification faithfulness , we evaluated 5,912 β \beta reward grantings, matching the number of workflow stages we annotated. The failure rate is presented in Table 3 . The results show that the overall failure rate in our evaluation is below 10%, which is relatively low when compared with previous efforts in formal reasoning LLM training ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) When taking a closer look at the detailed results, the failure cases show that most failures in predicate annotation occur in LLM-as-judge predicates, mainly due to ambiguity in the natural-language criteria relative to the workflow requirements. For workflow segmentation, most errors stem from ambiguity in segmentation. Due to the shared context across workflow stages and the relatively ambiguous indicators for each stage, the failure most commonly occurs in ambiguous cutting-point steps, such as the final verification of the last step, which can also be interpreted as a form of situation exploration for the next step. For trajectory verification, the most common failure pattern is a chunked context length of 16,384 tokens fed into the LLM judge, which, in some cases, results in context length overflow, causing the LLM judge to make judgments based on an incomplete context and leading to the failure. From the outstanding empirical results shown in Table 1 and the relatively steady increase in Figure 2 , there is no significant effect on training stability and performance at this error rate. A similar pattern was also observed on previous research on auto-formalization ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . To further examine the LLM-based faithfulness validator’s results, we sampled 60 examples per annotation type, for a total of 180 faithfulness annotations. Among them, only one annotation in Predicate Annotation is judged as having an error. In particular, it misclassifies one predicate coreCheckPatterns = "test" , which is the checker for normalized bash commands. The LLM annotator treated "test" as test-time-only at the verification level, whereas in practice it is used to test the program in execution. Furthermore, providing this additional context to the annotator does not change its judgment of the predicate annotation, which the authors have subsequently verified to be correct. Thus, we conclude that our evaluation method for the three types of faithfulness of LLM-based workflow annotation is reliable enough to support the conclusions we draw from it.

sections.heading: Appendix E Comparison Between Dependent-Type with Other Formal Languages
sections.text: In this section, we compare the dependent-type language we apply in the Lean4Agent and the Lean4AgenticRL framework with other commonly used formal languages for the specification and verification of agent behaviors. Firstly, dependent-type languages like Lean offer greater expressiveness for uniformly modeling and verifying the agent workflows and trajectories. Other formal languages, such as propositional temporal logics like LTL, reason over a sequence of atomic propositions, which means they cannot describe structured data such as nested tool-call arguments or JSON schemas, cannot relate values across different states, and are limited to regular properties. Although it can express counting constraints over loops, more complicated cases, such as every edit being matched by a later test run, fall outside the logic. Another commonly applied formal language is the Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) language, such as Z3 ( De Moura & Bjørner, 2008 ) . Although SMT solvers support recursive algebraic datatypes and recursive function definitions, their decision procedures are generally unable to prove the properties of self-referential definitions, since doing so requires induction, and some of the loop properties must be handled through induction. In contrast, dependent type formal languages provide inductive types for recursive structures such as nested JSON and workflow graphs, support induction to reason properties about loops and self-referential definitions, and value-dependent types that allow a stage’s pre- and post-conditions to be stated directly over the concrete data it consumes and produces, which is vital for self-verification behavior in agent executions. Furthermore, dependent type formal language also inherits the resolution of Russell’s paradox ( Kneale, 1971 ) through higher-order statements that quantify over predicates and workflows while preventing the self-pointing constructions that render naive set theory inconsistent, whereas LTL and first-order SMT solver languages avoid such paradoxes only by being too weak to express higher-order statements at all. Moreover, temporal formulas and SMT-decidable fragments can be embedded as definitions within Lean, thus a single dependent-type formal language can host all of these formalisms while relying on a small trusted kernel to verify their results. These advantages are why we chose to use Lean as a uniform backbone for formalizing agent behaviors and providing multi-level rewards for agentic RL.

sections.heading: Appendix F Discussion of Formal Boundary for Lean4AgenticRL
sections.text: Since Lean4AgenticRL still applies LLM-as-judge in many places of the framework, we discuss the boundary between formal verification and informal model behavior in this section. Due to the black-box nature of LLM policy, we are unable to directly verify the interior generation process for the agents. Instead, following Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , we aim to bound the agent’s behavior at each workflow stage by formulating pre- and post-conditions using the semantic predicate system. In particular, the formal boundary of the system is established after the problem-specific workflow has been formalized as Lean code, the execution trajectory has been segmented into workflow stages, and the annotation for LLM-as-judge predicates in the trajectory has been completed. These three steps are performed by LLMs and are unable to be formally guaranteed. Within the boundary, the Lean formulates the atomic predicates into a complex expression for modeling agent behaviors. Thus, the major source of informality in our system comes from errors in the LLM-as-judge annotation steps, which is detailed in Appendix D.2 . We apply this set of formal boundaries to balance the expressiveness and formal guarantees of our reward system, with informality limited to the workflow formalization and the predicate judgment process. This provides more fine-grained control than simple rule-based LLM-as-judge verification and verifies more properties than traditional pure formal methods.

sections.heading: Appendix G Benchmark and Task details
sections.text: SWE-Bench-Verified contains 500 human-verified issues drawn from 12 widely used Python repositories on GitHub. Given an issue description and a containerized repository, the agent must produce a Git patch that resolves the issue, and its correctness is determined by repository-level test cases. In contrast, TerminalBench-2.0/2.1 comprises 89 challenging terminal-based tasks spanning SWE, system administration, security, scientific computing, and other general domains. The agent completes each task from its natural-language descriptions by executing commands in the container, and success is assessed by task-specific tests of the final container state. Following common practice, we report mean@3 on SWE-Bench-Verified and mean@5 on both TerminalBench versions, all under randomized seeds. We checked all three evaluation sets against our training data and found no overlap.

sections.heading: H.1 Problem Specific Workflow Formalization
sections.text: This section provides a detailed explanation of how we formalize our problem-specific workflow as Lean code and verify it for Section 2.3.1 . We use one of several frontier models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Claude-Opus-4.6/4.8, GLM-5.2, and Kimi-K3), depending on availability, with Claude-code to transform the SWE problem-specific workflow (PSWF) 𝒲 S \mathcal{W}_{S} and its corresponding task statements into a static semantic verification schema in the Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) framework. The prompt for the formalization process is demonstrated in Figure 3 . We first construct the workflow schema, a graph whose nodes represent workflow stages and whose edges specify transitions, including retries and branches. Subsequently, we annotate the formal semantic representations by specifying the pre- and post-conditions for each stage, which specify the facts required before and after execution. It is supported by our enhanced predicate system, which is enriched in predicates in the SWE task and further extended to terminal-usage tasks. The predicate here represents the atomic properties for agent behaviors. In particular, the predicates represent variable-level properties of explicit variables in the workflows, information-level components that model the implicit information flowing in the process, and workflow-level predicates that model the high-level goals of the workflows. The transformation of the PSWF into Lean4Agent verifiable form enables verification of internal consistency and lays the foundation for granting rewards in subsequent stages.

sections.heading: H.2 Workflow Stage Segmentation
sections.text: This section details the process of our workflow segmentation. Its inputs are the PSWF, the formalized workflow, and the execution trajectory. The trajectory is a sequence of agent steps that include reasoning, tool calls, and their results. The agent step has no direct information about which workflow stage it belongs to. In this stage, we segment the trajectory into different stages. The details of the segmentation prompt are presented in Figure 4 .

sections.heading: I.1 β \beta Reward Annotation
sections.text: This section provides details of the method we used to annotate the β \beta reward. In particular, following Lean4Agent’s design, the β \beta rewards determine whether the required postconditions are established by the stage’s agent executions. For some predicates, we can verify them directly using Lean or Python code, while others may require LLM-as-judge verification. In particular, the latter handles properties that cannot be faithfully specified by programs. All the LLM judgments must be supported by observed evidence. The detailed annotation procedure is presented in Figure 5 .

sections.heading: I.2 γ \gamma Reward Annotation
sections.text: In this section, we introduce the symbolic rules we judge for γ \gamma rewards following Section 2.3.3 . We set the γ \gamma reward as a negative-only guard over each agent step. The detailed rules are as follows: 1. Consecutive repetition: This rule penalizes the third repeated back-to-back run of the same normalized bash command. 2. No-operation commands: It penalizes the command chains consisting of no-operations or delays such as exit, exit 0, true or numeric sleep x . 3. Constant shell output: It penalizes constant-only echo , printf , or print-only cat + constant string chains that neither inspect nor modify the task state. 4. General pure-print script: It penalizes the Python or other form of code snippets whose syntax tree contains only literal-valued print calls and no state-dependent executions. 5. Intermediate no-action: It penalizes the non-final agent step with no executable bash or tool actions to prevent the agent from inflating the step count with reasoning-only turns. 6. No-progress re-execution: It penalizes re-running the same bash command within a workflow stage with no environment-modifying tool calls. During training, fast Lean + Python code evaluates the above rules on the trajectory and automatically passes them to the reward server for uniform reward assignment. We use Python tools to parse the initial string into syntax trees, and we represent and verify its properties through predicates in Lean. In particular, we penalize only the steps, without rewarding the agent in γ \gamma , to avoid the reward itself becoming the source of hacking. In general, this set of rules can largely prevent the agent from hacking the rewards by inflating the number of steps the agent takes. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22448v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026 Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards Ruida Wang Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Gerald Friedland Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Tong Zhang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Chris Kong Affiliation: Amazon Web Services Abstract Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose Lean4AgenticRL , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. Lean4AgenticRL first builds a problem-specific workflow system that balances the agent’s own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using Lean4AgenticRL , we train LAR-9B/27B , a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of the similar size. LAR-27B achieves 77.3% on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by 9.89% and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by 5.07% . These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at Amazon Web Services. ‘ 2 2 footnotetext: Correspondence to: Chris Kong at luyankon@amazon.com . 1 Introduction The ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform long-running agentic tasks has been regarded as a key capability by the computer science community ( Wang et al., 2026b ) . This capability is typically evaluated by solving complex software engineering (SWE) ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) and terminal-usage ( Team, 2025c ) tasks within advanced harness frameworks ( Anthropic, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2025 ; Merrill & Shaw, 2025 ) . Given the significant practical value ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , training advanced agentic LLMs has become an important research direction. Agentic capability in LLMs refers to the model’s ability to actively interact with an environment to explore, understand, and resolve tasks. Previous works have developed multiple approaches to strengthen this ability, including simple prompting ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ) and building supervised fine-tuning datasets ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Badertdinov et al., 2026 ) . Building on the success of scaling Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2025 ) and multi-turn agentic RL methods ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ) , the community has driven significant progress in long-horizon agent tasks such as SWE and terminal-usage. Figure 1: Overview of Lean4AgenticRL framework: The Lean4AgenticRL framework contains three major steps: (a) Problem-specific workflow agent system : A plan-then-execute process that first explores and produces the problem-specific workflow (PSWF). Then execute the PSWF to solve the task. (b) Workflow Formalization and Multi-level Reward Annotation : An annotation process that formalizes the PSWF into our generalized Lean4Agent framework. Then segment the agent trajectory into workflow stages, and assign mid-level workflow-stage rewards and low-level toolcall rewards. (c) Lean4AgenticRL training : We apply the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithms to train the LLM agent with multi-level rewards. Despite significant progress in large-scale agentic RL, reliably assigning process rewards in long agent traces remains an open problem. In particular, current agentic RL methods ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Team et al., 2026 ) primarily rely on high-level outcome rewards, building on their success in single-turn RLVR. However, these signals do not directly distinguish useful intermediate actions from incorrect or redundant steps within successful trajectories, limiting the effectiveness of training ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . This has motivated the use of process rewards to supervise the agent’s intermediate steps ( Wang et al., 2026c ; Xi et al., 2026 ) . However, existing approaches often focus on low-level toolcall results, which may overlook broader workflow progress and degrade performance when a single toolcall cannot directly connect to the task objectives ( Modecrua et al., 2026 ) . Overall, these limitations highlight the need to unify the high-level outcome rewards, mid-level workflow-stage rewards, and low-level toolcall rewards in a verifiable way to enable more effective agentic RL. To address the above limitations, we propose Lean4AgenticRL , a unified framework for deriving multi-level rewards within a uniform, Lean4Agent verifiable, open-ended agentic RL setting. The overview of Lean4AgenticRL is presented in Figure 1 . In Lean4AgenticRL , we first use problem-specific workflow (PSWF) agent system that balances the agent’s inherent capabilities with execution controls through a plan-then-execute paradigm. It further provides the basis for verifying agent behaviors. Subsequently, we extend the Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) verification framework from fixed workflows to general harnesses. Then, we formalize the PSWF and segment the agent trajectories into formal workflow stages and annotate the trajectories with high-level outcome rewards ( α \alpha ), mid-level workflow-stage rewards ( β \beta ), and low-level toolcall rewards ( γ \gamma ). These reward signals synergistically support learning from both final outcomes and intermediate behaviors through our workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm, enabling more effective agentic RL. We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We propose Lean4AgenticRL , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards within Lean, a uniform dependent-type verifiable language, for agentic RL in open-ended domains that enables more effective agentic RL. (2) We develop problem-specific workflow and generalize the current agent verification framework from fixed workflow to general harness systems. They greatly enlarge the applicability of the current uniform formal agent verification system. (3) We train LAR-9B/27B through Lean4AgenticRL . Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of comparable size on SWE and general terminal-usage tasks. LAR-27B achieves 77.3% on TerminalBench-2.1 ( Team, 2025c ) and, across the three benchmarks we evaluated, our model outperforms their base model by 9.89% and the second-best models of comparable size by 5.07% on average. The performance highlights the effectiveness and generality of Lean4AgenticRL . Furthermore, Lean4AgenticRL offers a new view of agentic RL methods grounded in formal verification and provides a unified framework for future studies to explore applications of formal methods within the modern RL paradigm. To facilitate the advancement of the fields, our code and model have been open-sourced in https://github.com/RickySkywalker/Lean4AgenticRL 2 Methodology We detail the formulation of the Lean4AgenticRL framework in this section. The goal of Lean4AgenticRL is to derive multi-level rewards in a uniform Lean schema to achieve more effective agentic RL in open-ended domains. Section 2.1 introduces the key preliminaries, Section 2.2 details the formulation of Problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system, Section 2.3 introduces the workflow formalization and reward annotation method, and Section 2.4 shows how we train the model using the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO method. 2.1 Preliminaries In this section, we introduce the central preliminary concept for Lean4AgenticRL . Additionally, we present the definitions of the terms we used in the paper in Appendix B . LLM Agent Following ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , we define an LLM agent as an LLM-based system that cycles between reasoning with tool-based actions. The reasoning enables the agent to formulate, track, and revise its plan, while actions allow it to interact with environments to execute external tools or read information sources. In our paper, we use Claude-code ( Anthropic, 2026a ) or Terminus-2 ( Merrill & Shaw, 2025 ) as our agent harness. Lean4Agent Verification System Following Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , we present the workflow for the LLM agent as a heterogeneous directed graph 𝒢 = ⟨ V , E ⟩ \mathcal{G}=\langle V,E\rangle , where V := { v i } i = 1 m V:=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} contains the workflow stages and E ⊆ V × V E\subseteq V\times V specifies the allowed transitions between stages. The Lean4Agent system implements a set of pre-conditions ρ i ( p ​ r ​ e ) \rho_{i}^{(pre)} and post-conditions ρ i ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho_{i}^{(post)} with the predicates , which describe atomic properties of the agent behaviors. When executing the workflow, we obtain trajectory 𝝉 \bm{\tau} , and each stage i ∈ [ 1 , m ] i\in[1,m] has its trajectory 𝝉 i = { τ i , j } \bm{\tau}_{i}=\{\tau_{i,j}\} . The trajectory-level verification evaluates whether its entry and exit states satisfy ρ i ( p ​ r ​ e ) \rho_{i}^{(pre)} and ρ i ( p ​ o ​ s ​ t ) \rho_{i}^{(post)} , respectively. These predicate-based specifications, combined with a dependent-type formal foundation, provide the verification of workflow-level coherence and assess completion of the specified stages’ goals. Following Lean4Agent, in this work, we define a stage as verified when its Lean4Agent workflow specification’s post-condition holds over after the stage’s execution. 2.2 Problem-specific Workflow Agent System This section introduces the problem-specific workflow (PSWF) system. It aims to balance the controllability of fixed-workflow execution against the flexibility of free-form, ReAct-style execution. It also lays the foundation for our further verification process. In particular, we achieve this by a plan-then-execute paradigm. 2.2.1 Planning Phase In this phase, we apply the LLM as the planning agent within the agent harness to explore the task environment and formulate a PSWF. Formally, given the problem statement 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , its environment ℰ \mathcal{E} (commonly a container), and a general workflow 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , we obtain the PSWF 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{S}} as follows: 𝒲 𝒮 , 𝝉 ( p ) = H ​ ( L ​ L ​ M ​ ( ℰ , 𝒮 , 𝒲 ) ) \mathcal{W_{S}},\bm{\tau}^{(p)}=\text{H}(LLM(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W})) where H ( ⋅ ) (\cdot) denotes the agent harness and 𝝉 ( p ) \bm{\tau}^{(p)} denotes the trajectory for planning phase. The 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W_{S}} is a natural-language plan that specializes in stage-wise guidance in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} based on the findings from its exploration. For example, in SWE tasks, it contains detailed information such as relevant source files, suspected causes of the issue, and proposed repair and verification steps, providing concrete instructions for subsequent execution. The PSWF aims to control the agent behavior without limiting its flexibility. 2.2.2 Execution Phase In this phase, we execute the PSWF 𝒲 𝒮 \mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{S}} in its task environment ℰ \mathcal{E} by instructing the LLM agent. To avoid repeated exploration, we also include the planning-phase trajectory 𝝉 ( p ) \bm{\tau}^{(p)} in the context. Alongside the planning phase, we complete the rollout of our agentic RL and lay the foundation for subsequent multi-reward assignment based on the agent verification system. 2.3 Workflow Formalization and Multi-level Reward Annotation In this section, we introduce methods for adapting a formal verification system beyond a fixed workflow schema via the PSWF formalization, and detail methods for annotating multi-level rewards based on the formalized workflow and execution trajectory. 2.3.1 Generalizing Agent Verification System with PSWF The current agent verification framework that can uniformly process both workflow and trajectory levels, such as Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , is designed for predefined, fixed workflows. It was first scaled by OpenAI-O1 ( OpenAI, 2024 ) and open-sourced by DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and Kimi-K1.5 ( Team et al., 2025 ) . RLVR shows that simple verifier-based outcome rewards can elicit reasoning capabilities without learning reward models. Building on this paradigm, agentic RL extends it to multi-turn agent interactions, typically rewarding the correctness of the final answer or task success ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ) . However, as the agent’s task extends over a longer horizon, sparse outcome rewards that assign identical credit to every step cannot distinguish useful intermediate actions from redundant or erroneous ones. To provide denser training signals, subsequent studies apply process rewards on individual tool calls or infer step-level rewards from LLM judges ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . However, these signals are largely tied to low-level tool calls, which overlook broader progress and may even impair optimization ( Modecrua et al., 2026 ) . Prior work on hierarchical credit assignment ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) relies on highly similar trajectories or tree-search methods, a setting that differs substantially from open-ended tasks such as SWE and general terminal usage. A separate line of work replaces LLM judges with symbolic or algorithmic oracles as verifiable process rewards, but those oracles act as task-specific verifiers in controlled environments ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . In contrast, Lean4AgenticRL derives verifiable rewards across multiple levels under a unified formal language framework for general, open-ended agent executions. 4.2 Verifiable Agent Systems As agentic systems mature and are increasingly deployed in high-stakes, long-horizon tasks, a growing line of work aims to formally model and verify agent behaviors. Some frameworks provide a type-based linter for the agent workflow that is embedded in agent languages ( Chase, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , while others verify tool calls and their execution results ( Miculicich et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) . More recently, Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) formalizes agent behavior from workflow to execution in Lean, but it relies on predefined, fixed workflow settings. In contrast to theorem proving ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) and code verification ( Li et al., 2026 ) , where formal verifiers routinely supply training signals, these agent verifications serve only as runtime checks or post-hoc audits. 5 Conclusion This paper presents Lean4AgenticRL , to the best of our knowledge, the first framework that derives multi-level process rewards under a unified framework based on Lean4, an expressive dependent-type formal language, for open-ended agentic RL. Its problem-specific workflow agent system balances the agent’s inherent capability with execution controllability. Lean4AgenticRL proposes the workflow formalization methods that extend agent verification beyond fixed workflows to general harnesses. Built on this foundation, Lean4AgenticRL unifies high-level outcome rewards ( α \alpha ), mid-level workflow-stage rewards ( β \beta ), and low-level toolcall rewards ( γ \gamma ). It also proposes the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm, which aims to resolve the grouping problem in agentic RL. We train the LAR-9B/27B models using Lean4AgenticRL . Extensive experiments on SWE-Bench-Verified, TerminalBench-2.0, and 2.1 indicate that they outperform their base models by an average of 9.89% and the second-best model we know on those domains by 5.07% . To the best of our knowledge, LAR-9B/27B achieves the best results among models with comparable size. More broadly, Lean4AgenticRL lays a foundation for integrating verifiable symbolic signals into LLM training and points towards a new paradigm for agentic RL. References Anthropic (2026a) Anthropic. Firstly, Lean4AgenticRL ’s verifiability still relies on explicitly bounding agent behavior externally; it does not open the black box of LLM’s internal computation to achieve thorough and transparent verification. Appendix B Term Definitions Since the verifiable agent framework through dependent-type language like Lean is a new domain that may not be widely known by the community, we present the definition of the terms in this section: 1. Lean 4: Lean 4 is a functional programming language and interactive theorem prover based on dependent type theory, whose trusted kernel mechanically checks the correctness of programs and proofs; in Lean4AgenticRL , leveraging the foundation library established in Lean4Agent 2.3.1 , we use it as the shared formal foundation for building formal representations for workflows and unifying the multi-level reward signals. 2. Dependent type language: A dependent type language, such as Lean, allows types to depend on values, so that a single language can express both programs and precise mathematical statements about them, and, under the Curry-Howard correspondence ( Sørensen & Urzyczyn, 2006 ) , verifying a proof reduces to type-checking a term against the type of the statement it proves. 3. D.2 Faithfulness of Workflow Annotation In this section, we evaluate the faithfulness of our LLM-based annotations during Lean4AgenticRL . In particular, we have the following three main parts of LLM-as-judge annotation in our framework: • Predicate annotation faithfulness: In this type of faithfulness, we evaluate whether the generated workflow in our problem-specific workflow (PSWF) stage has the correct workflow annotation. In particular, we evaluate whether it annotates correct pre- and post-conditions using the correct predicate. The annotation fails in this step if it misses some important predicates. For example, if the acceptance_criteria predicate required by the PSWF is missing from the postcondition of the corresponding workflow stage, the annotation is counted as a failure. • Workflow segmentation faithfulness: This type of faithfulness mainly verifies whether our segmentation process faithfully segmented the execution tool calls into the corresponding general workflow steps. The annotation fails at this step if the segmentation of tool calls spans significantly different workflow steps. For example, if one tool call in SWE agents is writing patches to fix the program, but it is classified as the write_test workflow stage, then it is a failure. • Trajectory verification faithfulness: It mainly covers the faithfulness of the process for our actual annotation of β \beta rewards with the trajectory. One annotation is counted as a failure if this workflow stage is judged a failure by a human/external LLM judge, but it provides β \beta rewards during training and vice versa. For example, if the implement_fix workflow step fails to generate a correct fix for the SWE workflow, but in the training Lean4AgenticRL reward judgments provide β \beta reward to that step, then it is counted as a failure. Appendix E Comparison Between Dependent-Type with Other Formal Languages In this section, we compare the dependent-type language we apply in the Lean4Agent and the Lean4AgenticRL framework with other commonly used formal languages for the specification and verification of agent behaviors. Firstly, dependent-type languages like Lean offer greater expressiveness for uniformly modeling and verifying the agent workflows and trajectories. Other formal languages, such as propositional temporal logics like LTL, reason over a sequence of atomic propositions, which means they cannot describe structured data such as nested tool-call arguments or JSON schemas, cannot relate values across different states, and are limited to regular properties. Although it can express counting constraints over loops, more complicated cases, such as every edit being matched by a later test run, fall outside the logic. Another commonly applied formal language is the Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) language, such as Z3 ( De Moura & Bjørner, 2008 ) . Although SMT solvers support recursive algebraic datatypes and recursive function definitions, their decision procedures are generally unable to prove the properties of self-referential definitions, since doing so requires induction, and some of the loop properties must be handled through induction. In contrast, dependent type formal languages provide inductive types for recursive structures such as nested JSON and workflow graphs, support induction to reason properties about loops and self-referential definitions, and value-dependent types that allow a stage’s pre- and post-conditions to be stated directly over the concrete data it consumes and produces, which is vital for self-verification behavior in agent executions. Furthermore, dependent type formal language also inherits the resolution of Russell’s paradox ( Kneale, 1971 ) through higher-order statements that quantify over predicates and workflows while preventing the self-pointing constructions that render naive set theory inconsistent, whereas LTL and first-order SMT solver languages avoid such paradoxes only by being too weak to express higher-order statements at all. Moreover, temporal formulas and SMT-decidable fragments can be embedded as definitions within Lean, thus a single dependent-type formal language can host all of these formalisms while relying on a small trusted kernel to verify their results. These advantages are why we chose to use Lean as a uniform backbone for formalizing agent behaviors and providing multi-level rewards for agentic RL. Appendix F Discussion of Formal Boundary for Lean4AgenticRL Since Lean4AgenticRL still applies LLM-as-judge in many places of the framework, we discuss the boundary between formal verification and informal model behavior in this section. Due to the black-box nature of LLM policy, we are unable to directly verify the interior generation process for the agents. Instead, following Lean4Agent ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , we aim to bound the agent’s behavior at each workflow stage by formulating pre- and post-conditions using the semantic predicate system. In particular, the formal boundary of the system is established after the problem-specific workflow has been formalized as Lean code, the execution trajectory has been segmented into workflow stages, and the annotation for LLM-as-judge predicates in the trajectory has been completed. These three steps are performed by LLMs and are unable to be formally guaranteed. Within the boundary, the Lean formulates the atomic predicates into a complex expression for modeling agent behaviors. Thus, the major source of informality in our system comes from errors in the LLM-as-judge annotation steps, which is detailed in Appendix D.2 . We apply this set of formal boundaries to balance the expressiveness and formal guarantees of our reward system, with informality limited to the workflow formalization and the predicate judgment process. This provides more fine-grained control than simple rule-based LLM-as-judge verification and verifies more properties than traditional pure formal methods. Appendix G Benchmark and Task details SWE-Bench-Verified contains 500 human-verified issues drawn from 12 widely used Python repositories on GitHub. Given an issue description and a containerized repository, the agent must produce a Git patch that resolves the issue, and its correctness is determined by repository-level test cases. In contrast, TerminalBench-2.0/2.1 comprises 89 challenging terminal-based tasks spanning SWE, system administration, security, scientific computing, and other general domains. The agent completes each task from its natural-language descriptions by executing commands in the container, and success is assessed by task-specific tests of the final container state. Following common practice, we report mean@3 on SWE-Bench-Verified and mean@5 on both TerminalBench versions, all under randomized seeds. We checked all three evaluation sets against our training data and found no overlap.
